query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing Mo with Nb in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy to form an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will reduce its overall density without compromising its key mechanical properties at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and established high strength and high-temperature creep resistance.
generation.intervention: Substitute molybdenum (Mo) with an equivalent atomic fraction of niobium (Nb) to yield a HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under tensile and creep loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (approximately 1000 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a homogeneous high-entropy solid-solution microstructure with similar lattice distortion and potential precipitation behavior that mediates strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a lower density compared to Mo yet is chemically and structurally similar enough to maintain high configurational entropy and lattice distortion. This substitution is expected to lower the average density while preserving the solid solution strengthening and high-temperature stability (including creep resistance) by maintaining the necessary phase stability and microstructural features.
generation.predicted_outcome: A moderate decrease in density (on the order of approximately 5–15% reduction, subject to experimental confirmation) compared to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr while maintaining comparable tensile strength and creep resistance at both room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with its reported density and mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions typical for high-temperature structural applications, specifically testing up to around 1000 °C and using standard tensile/creep loading regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the density decrease and any minor impacts on phase stability or subtle changes in the mechanical performance remain to be quantified experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the proposed equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy using the same casting procedures as for HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize the microstructure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to verify phase stability. Measure density via the Archimedes method. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and creep tests at approximately 1000 °C to evaluate mechanical properties.
measurements: XRD and SEM for phase and microstructural analysis
Elevated temperature (≈1000 °C) creep resistance (e.g., creep rate or rupture time)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the substituted alloy fails to exhibit a statistically significant reduction in density (e.g., less than a 5% decrease compared to 10.21 g/cm³) or if its room temperature tensile strength or high-temperature creep resistance deteriorates by over approximately 10% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Among the various systems of alloying elements studied, the Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 alloy seems to be attractive due to its reduced density of 9.94 g/cm 3 [ [2] , [3] ], few publications [ [4] , [5] , [6] ] deal with thr thermodynamic properties of certain compositions of the Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti.
